title: What materials are like, and why smooth things shine

summary.text: Breathe on a cold steel plate, and for a moment it goes dull. A few seconds later it shines again. Your child touches, presses, bends and looks at things around the home. They find words for what a material is like: hard or soft, rough or smooth, bendy or stiff, shiny or dull. With a torch, they find that the shiny things all have a very smooth surface.
summary.art: A girl breathing a misty cloud onto a steel plate while her mother holds a torch, and a bright spot of light on the wall behind them.

intro.hook: Look at a steel plate. Now breathe 'haaa' on it. Where did the shine go?
intro.text: The plate was shiny. Your breath made a misty patch, and the patch looked dull. Then the mist went away, and the shine came back. The plate was steel all the time. In this unit you find out what makes a thing shiny or dull. You also find out how things feel when you touch, press and bend them.
intro.art: A close-up of a shiny steel plate with a small misty patch in the middle, and a child's face leaning in to look.

outcomes: By the end I can say if a thing is hard or soft, rough or smooth, bendy or stiff, and shiny or dull, by pressing, touching, bending and looking.
By the end I can say that these words tell us what a material is like. They are called properties.
By the end I can say that shiny things have a very smooth surface, which sends light back in one direction.
By the end I can show that the same paper can be bendy or stiff, depending on its shape.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of. Steel, wood, paper, cloth, glass and plastic are materials.
terms.example: A tumbler is a thing. Steel is the material it is made of.
terms.art: A steel tumbler, a wooden spoon and a cotton hanky in a row, each with a small label under it: steel, wood, cotton.

terms.meaning: A property is what a material is like. Hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stiff, shiny and dull are properties.
terms.example: A pillow is soft. Soft is one of its properties.
terms.art: A child pressing a pillow with one hand and knocking on a wooden table with the other.

terms.meaning: The surface is the outside of a thing, the part you touch.
terms.example: The surface of a coconut is rough and hairy.
terms.art: A child's fingers stroking the hairy brown surface of a coconut.

terms.meaning: When light bounces off a thing, we say the thing reflects the light. Smooth things reflect light back in one direction, so they shine.
terms.example: A steel plate reflects torch light onto the wall as a bright spot.
terms.art: A torch shining on a tilted steel plate, and a bright round spot of light on the wall.

explanations.concept: Properties: words for what a material is like
explanations.definition: A property is what a material is like. We find properties by touching, pressing, bending and looking.
explanations.description: A steel spoon is hard, smooth, stiff and shiny. A cotton towel is soft, a little rough, bendy and dull. You find these with your own body: fingers stroke, a thumb presses, hands bend and eyes look.
examples: A coconut shell is hard and rough.
A banana leaf is bendy, smooth and shiny.
A chalk stick is hard, dull and stiff. It snaps if you bend it.
explanations.context: This card says what a property is, and how you find one.
explanations.art: A steel spoon and a folded cotton towel side by side, with four small hands around them: one pressing, one stroking, one bending, and an eye looking.

explanations.concept: Hard and soft, rough and smooth
explanations.definition: A soft thing changes shape when you press it. A hard thing does not. A rough surface has bumps you can feel. A smooth surface feels flat and even.
explanations.description: Press your thumb into a pillow. It squashes, so it is soft. A steel tumbler does not squash, so it is hard. A coconut shell has bumps and hairs you can feel, so it is rough. A glass bottle feels flat, so it is smooth.
examples: Idli batter is soft. A spoon goes in easily.
A floor tile is hard and smooth. A coir doormat is hard and rough.
The torn edge of a sheet of paper shows tiny threads, called fibres, like little hairs.
explanations.context: This card is about what your thumb and fingers found in the Touch Hunt.
explanations.art: A thumb pressing into a fluffy pillow, a thumb on a steel tumbler, a finger on a hairy coconut shell and a finger on a glass bottle.

explanations.concept: Bendy and stiff: shape matters too
explanations.definition: A bendy thing bends easily. A stiff thing keeps its shape when you push it. The same material can be bendy or stiff, depending on its shape.
explanations.description: Lay a sheet of paper across two books, and it sags. Fold the same paper into a zigzag, like a fan, and it holds coins. Nothing was added, only the shape changed. A thin steel wire bends easily, but a thick steel spoon is stiff.
examples: In the paper bridge test, a flat sheet sagged under one coin. The zigzag sheet held many coins.
Cardboard boxes have a wavy layer of paper inside, which makes them stiff.
A banana leaf bends easily, but the thick stem down its middle is stiff.
explanations.context: This card is about the paper bridge test, where you folded paper to make it stiff.
explanations.art: Two paper bridges between two stacks of books: a flat sheet sagging under one coin, and a zigzag-folded sheet holding a pile of coins.

explanations.definition: Light bounces off most things we see. A very smooth surface reflects light back in one direction, so it shines. A rough surface sends light off in many directions, so it looks dull.
explanations.description: Shine a torch at a steel plate, and a bright spot jumps onto the wall. Smooth steel sends the light back in one direction. A cloth's tiny threads send it off in all directions, so no spot comes. Your breath leaves tiny drops of water on a cold plate. The drops make it bumpy, so it goes dull until they dry.
examples: In the Torch Spot Test, the steel plate, the mirror and the bowl of still water made a bright spot. The cloth and the newspaper did not.
When you splash still water, the bright spot breaks into wobbly pieces.
A polished wooden table shines. Rough, unpolished wood looks dull.
explanations.context: This card says why some things shine. It is what you found in the Torch Spot Test.
explanations.art: Two side-by-side pictures: torch light hitting a smooth plate and bouncing off as one neat beam, and torch light hitting a bumpy cloth and scattering in many little arrows.

agreed.text: A thing shines when its surface is very smooth.
agreed.evidence: Smooth steel, glass and still water make a bright torch spot. Mist, ripples or scratches make the same things duller. People polish metal to make it shine.

agreed.text: We can find a material's properties with our senses.
agreed.evidence: Pressing, stroking, bending and looking tell us hard or soft, rough or smooth, bendy or stiff, and shiny or dull. Different people testing the same thing find the same answers.

agreed.text: The shape of a thing changes how bendy it is.
agreed.evidence: A flat sheet of paper sags. Folded into a zigzag, the same paper holds coins. Cardboard and tin roofs use folds and waves to be stiff.

challenging.who: A common idea among children, and many grown-ups too
challenging.for: Steel plates, kitchen foil, gold earrings and brass lamps all shine.
challenging.against: Still water, glass, a glazed cup, a banana leaf and a polished wooden table shine too. They are not metal. What they share is a very smooth surface.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that only metal shines.

challenging.who: A common idea among young children
challenging.for: A steel tumbler can be dropped many times and stays whole.
challenging.against: A glass tumbler is hard, but it can shatter when dropped. A soft cotton rope does not shatter. Hard means it does not squash when you press it. It does not mean it cannot break.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that hard means unbreakable.

challenging.claim: A smooth surface has no bumps at all.
challenging.who: What our fingers seem to tell us
challenging.for: A sheet of paper or a mirror feels perfectly flat to a finger.
challenging.against: Under a magnifying glass, paper is a tangle of fibres. Even a mirror has bumps, far too small to see. Smooth only means the bumps are very small.
challenging.context: This card is about what smooth really means.

big_questions.q: A thick steel spoon is stiff, but a thin steel wire bends. Is stiffness in the steel, or in the shape?
big_questions.hint: It is the same steel. What is different about the two?

big_questions.q: Paper feels smooth to your finger. Would an ant find the paper smooth, as she walks across?
big_questions.hint: An ant is tiny. The fibres in paper might be like logs and hills to her.

big_questions.q: Is the shine in the plate, in the light, or in your eyes?
big_questions.hint: In a dark room the plate does not shine. With your eyes shut you see no shine. What does shine need?

big_questions.q: A pillow feels soft to you. Would it feel soft to an elephant? Or to a mosquito?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is pressing, and how hard.

story.title: The Grey Mirror
story.note: Aranmula is a real village in Kerala, beside the Pampa river. Families there make mirrors of polished metal, called Aranmula kannadi. Kannadi means mirror in Malayalam. Achamma means father's mother. Meenu and Achamma are made up.
text: Meenu was six. She lived in Aranmula, a village in Kerala beside the Pampa river. Her grandmother, Achamma, made mirrors.
They were not glass mirrors. Achamma made mirrors out of metal. People came from far away to buy them. They are called Aranmula kannadi.
One morning, Achamma lifted a round metal disc out of a clay mould. It was grey and dull, like an old pot.
Meenu looked into the disc. She saw no face. No eyes, no nose, no plaits.
'Achamma, that is not a mirror,' said Meenu. 'I can't see myself in it.'
'Not yet,' said Achamma. 'Touch it.'
Meenu ran her finger across the disc. It was hard and cold. It felt a little rough, like the back of a dosa tawa.
'It is full of tiny bumps,' said Achamma. 'Each bump sends the light off a different way. So no picture of you comes back.'
Achamma sat on the verandah with the disc, a soft cloth and a very fine powder. She rubbed, round and round. Meenu rubbed too, until her arms ached. Achamma kept going.
The next day, Meenu looked again. The disc had a grey glow. She saw a blur, the shape of a head.
'Is that me?' she asked.
'That is you, coming slowly,' said Achamma. 'Every day the bumps get smaller.'
Achamma rubbed for many days. One evening she held the disc up to the window.
Meenu looked in, and there she was. Her two eyes. Her two plaits. The gap where her front teeth had fallen out.
'It's me!' Meenu shouted. 'Achamma, what did you put on it?'
'Nothing,' said Achamma. 'It is the same metal. I only made its surface smooth. Smoother than your finger can feel.'
Meenu touched the mirror again. It felt cool and flat and even, with no bumps she could feel.
Achamma smiled. 'Now you know how a mirror is made.'
Meenu leaned close to the mirror and said 'Haaa.' A white mist covered her face. The mirror went dull.
'Oh no! I spoiled it!'
Achamma laughed. 'Watch.'
The mist shrank from the edges, like a cloud going away. Meenu's face came back, bright and clear.
'Your breath left tiny drops of water on top,' said Achamma. 'For a moment, the surface was bumpy again. Then the drops dried, and the smooth metal shone.'
In the evening, Meenu and Achamma walked to the river. The Pampa was still, and it shone like Achamma's mirror. The whole pink sky was in the water.
A long boat went past. Ripples spread out, and the sky in the river broke into a hundred pieces.
Meenu held Achamma's hand, and they waited. Slowly the river smoothed itself, and the sky came back.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meenu finds that the dull grey disc and the bright mirror are the same metal. Polishing only made its surface smooth. Her breath and a boat's ripples make smooth things bumpy for a moment, so they go dull, and they shine again when they are smooth.
ask: Why could Meenu not see herself in the grey disc at first?
What did Achamma put on the disc to make it a mirror?
Why did the mirror go dull when Meenu breathed on it? Why did it shine again?
Why did the sky in the river break into pieces when the boat went past?
art: A grandmother in a white mundu and blouse on a Kerala verandah, holding up a dull grey metal disc while a girl with two plaits peers into it.
The grandmother and the girl side by side, rubbing the disc round and round with soft cloths.
The girl laughing at her own clear face in a round metal mirror, with a little white mist fading from the edges.
A girl and her grandmother at the edge of a still river at sunset, the pink sky reflected in the water, and a long boat leaving ripples.

experiments.title: The Torch Spot Test: which things are shiny, and why?
experiments.context: In this experiment you shine a torch on things from home, in a dim room. A shiny thing throws a bright spot of light onto the wall. Then you try to make a shiny thing dull, and a dull-looking thing shine.
experiments.question: Which of these things will throw a bright spot of torch light onto the wall? What is the same about the ones that do?
experiments.predict: Guess first. For each thing, say: shiny or dull? Will it make a bright spot on the wall? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each thing gets the same torch, held at the same slant, about one ruler away. The room stays equally dim. We touch each thing in the same way, with one finger.

materials.item: a torch, or the torch on a phone
a steel plate, kept in the fridge for 10 minutes before you start
a small mirror with a frame or smooth edges
a flat sheet of kitchen foil, or a shiny steel lid
a sheet of newspaper
a cotton hanky or towel
a wooden spoon or rolling pin
a dark bowl, a dark plate with a rim, or a bucket, with water in it

schedule.what: Guess, shine the torch on each thing, touch each one, then breathe on the cold plate and look at still water.

experiments.record: Draw each thing. Draw a little sun next to the ones that made a bright spot. Draw a wavy line next to the ones that felt rough.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Yes, a spot on the ceiling

setup.art: A dim room with curtains drawn. A steel plate lies on a table near a pale wall, and a woman holds a torch at a slant above the plate.
setup.caption: 1. Make the room dim. Shine the torch at a slant onto each thing.

setup.art: A bright round spot of light on the wall above a steel plate, and a girl pointing at it with delight.
setup.caption: 2. Look at the wall and ceiling. Is there a bright spot?

setup.art: A girl breathing a misty patch onto a cold steel plate while the torch shines on it, and the spot on the wall gone faint.
setup.caption: 3. Breathe on the cold plate. What happens to the spot?

flow.do: 1. Put the steel plate in the fridge 10 minutes before you start. 2. Draw the curtains or switch off the lights. 3. Shine the torch on a pale wall.
flow.say: We are going to test which things are shiny. First, look. This is the torch's light on the wall.
flow.kid: Look at the torch light on the wall. Soon you will test some things.
flow.parent: A dim room makes the spots easy to see. Evening, with the lights off, works well. Keep the steel plate in the fridge until step 4.

flow.do: 1. Hold up each thing, one at a time. The steel plate stays in the fridge, so just say its name. You will show it in step 4. 2. Ask your child to guess. 3. Write their guesses in the table.
flow.say: Here are a mirror, foil, newspaper, a hanky, a wooden spoon, a steel plate and a bowl of water. For each one, is it shiny or dull? Will it make a bright spot on the wall? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at each thing. Shiny or dull? Will it make a bright spot? Why?

good: The mirror will make a spot, because I can see my face in it.
The hanky won't, because cloth doesn't shine.
The water won't, because water is not shiny.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Don't say what will happen. Many children guess that water will not make a spot.

flow.do: 1. Lay the mirror, foil, newspaper, hanky and wooden spoon flat on the table, one at a time, near the wall. 2. Hold the torch at a slant, about one ruler away. 3. Look for a bright spot on the wall or ceiling. 4. Your child strokes each thing with one finger. The steel plate waits for the next step.
flow.say: Let's shine the torch on the mirror. Look at the wall. Do you see a bright spot? Now touch the mirror. Is it smooth or rough?
flow.kid: Look at the wall. Do you see a bright spot? Now touch the thing. Smooth or rough?

ask.q: Which things made a bright spot?
good: The mirror and the foil.
The newspaper and the hanky made no spot.

flow.parent: Tilt each thing a little, or move the torch, until you find the spot. The mirror gives the brightest spot. Newspaper feels smooth but makes no spot. That is because it has bumps too small to feel.

flow.do: 1. Take the cold steel plate from the fridge. 2. Shine the torch on it and find the spot. Your child strokes the plate with one finger. 3. Your child breathes 'haaa' onto the plate. 4. Watch the spot, then watch the plate for a few seconds.
flow.say: Here is the cold steel plate. See its bright spot? Now breathe on the plate, 'haaa'. What happens to the spot? Keep watching.
flow.kid: Breathe 'haaa' on the cold plate. Watch the spot on the wall. Keep watching.

good: The plate went misty and the spot went faint.
Then the mist went away and the spot came back.

flow.parent: A cold plate mists up well and clears in a few seconds. The mist is tiny drops of water from the breath. In humid weather the cold plate may mist by itself when you take it out. Wipe it dry with a cloth, then shine the torch. A scratched plate gives a fainter spot than the mirror, which is fine. After the breath, wait, and the shine comes back as the plate warms.

flow.do: 1. Put the dark bowl of water on the table and let it go still. 2. Shine the torch onto the water at a slant. 3. Look for a spot on the ceiling or wall. 4. Your child gently touches the water once.
flow.say: Now the water. Did you guess it would make a spot? Let's look. Now touch the water once with one finger. Watch the spot.
flow.kid: Shine the torch on still water. Look up. Now touch the water once. Watch.

ask.q: What happened when you touched the water?
good: The spot wobbled and broke into pieces.
When the water went still, the spot came back.

flow.parent: Use a dark bowl or a bucket, not a steel bowl, so that only the water shines. Still water gives a fainter spot than the mirror, so keep the room dim. Ripples break it up. This shows that even water shines when its surface is smooth.

flow.do: Ask your child what was the same about each thing that made a spot. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Think about the mirror, the cold plate and the still water. What was the same about each thing that made a bright spot?
flow.kid: What was the same about all the things that made a spot?

good: They were all very smooth.
When they got bumpy, like with mist or ripples, the spot went.

check.q: The cold plate went dull when you breathed on it. Why?
options: Tiny drops of water made its surface bumpy
The steel turned into a different material
check.why: Your breath left tiny drops of water on the steel. The drops made the surface bumpy, so the light went off in many directions. When the drops dried, the smooth steel shone again.

flow.parent: Let your child say their own idea first. Then say the explanation: smooth surfaces reflect light back in one direction.

experiments.title: The Paper Bridge: can a fold make paper stiff?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a bridge from one sheet of paper, between two piles of books. You count how many coins the bridge holds. Then you fold the same kind of paper into a zigzag and test again.
experiments.question: Paper is bendy. Can we make the same paper stiff, just by folding it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many coins will a flat paper bridge hold? How many will a zigzag bridge hold? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both bridges use the same kind of paper, the same size. The book piles stay the same distance apart. We use the same coins, and put them gently in the middle each time.
results_table: Coins it held before it sagged

materials.item: 2 sheets from an old notebook, or 2 pages of newspaper cut to the same size
books, to make two piles of the same height
about 20 coins of the same kind, such as 1-rupee coins

schedule.what: Make a flat bridge and a zigzag bridge, and count the coins each holds.

experiments.record: Draw the flat bridge and the zigzag bridge. Under each, write or draw how many coins it held.

setup.art: Two piles of books on the floor, a hand-width apart, with a flat sheet of paper laid across them and sagging under a single coin.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a flat sheet across two piles of books. Add coins.

setup.art: A hand folding a sheet of paper back and forth into a zigzag, like a fan.
setup.caption: 2. Fold another sheet into a zigzag, like a fan.

setup.art: The zigzag paper laid across the same two piles of books, holding a neat pile of coins.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the zigzag across the books. Add coins one by one.

flow.do: 1. Make two piles of books, the same height, a hand-width apart. 2. Lay one flat sheet across them. 3. Ask your child to guess.
flow.say: This paper is our bridge. How many coins will it hold before it sags down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the paper bridge. How many coins will it hold? Why?

good: Not many, because paper is bendy.
Lots, because coins are small.

flow.do: Your child puts coins gently on the middle of the flat bridge, one at a time. Count until it sags down.
flow.say: Put one coin in the middle, gently. And another. Count with me. When does it sag down?
flow.kid: Put coins in the middle, one at a time. Count. When does it sag?
flow.parent: A flat sheet usually sags under one or two coins, or even under none.

flow.do: 1. Fold the second sheet back and forth into a zigzag, like a hand fan. Make the folds about two fingers wide. 2. Lay it across the books, with the folds running from one pile to the other.
flow.say: Now we fold this paper into a zigzag, back and forth. It is the same paper. How many coins will it hold now? Why?
flow.kid: Fold the paper back and forth, like a fan. Guess again. How many coins now?
flow.parent: Help with the folds. The folds must go from one pile of books to the other, not across.

flow.do: Your child puts coins on the zigzag bridge, gently and spread along the middle, one at a time, and counts.
flow.say: Add the coins, one at a time. Count with me. Is it sagging yet?
flow.kid: Add coins one at a time. Count. Is it sagging yet?
flow.parent: A zigzag of notebook paper often holds 10 coins or more. If the zigzag tips over, hold its ends flat on the books with two more books.

flow.do: Ask your child what changed, and then the check question.
flow.say: We used the same paper. What was different? Why do you think the zigzag held more?
flow.kid: Same paper. What was different? Why did the zigzag hold more?

good: The shape. The folds made it stiff.
It stood up in waves, so it did not bend.

check.q: Why did the zigzag bridge hold more coins?
options: Its folds made the paper stiff
Zigzag paper is a different material
check.why: The paper was the same material. Folding it into a zigzag changed its shape, and that made it stiff.

activities.title: The Touch Hunt: find a hard, soft, rough and smooth thing
activities.context: In this activity you hunt around your home. You press things to find hard and soft ones, and stroke things to find rough and smooth ones.

materials.item: a basket, a bag or a steel plate to collect things in
4 small paper slips with the words HARD, SOFT, ROUGH and SMOOTH, or 4 drawings: a stone, a pillow, a coconut and a glass

schedule.what: Hunt for things, press and stroke them, and put each one by the right slip.

activities.record: Draw one hard thing, one soft thing, one rough thing and one smooth thing.

setup.art: Four paper slips on the floor reading HARD, SOFT, ROUGH and SMOOTH, each with a tiny drawing.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the four word slips.

setup.art: A boy pressing his thumb into a cushion while his older sister strokes a coconut shell.
setup.caption: 2. Press to find hard or soft. Stroke to find rough or smooth.

flow.do: 1. Write HARD, SOFT, ROUGH and SMOOTH on the four slips, and lay them on the floor. 2. Show your child how to press with a thumb and how to stroke with a finger.
flow.say: We are hunting for things. Press with your thumb. Does it squash? Then it is soft. Stroke it with your finger. Can you feel bumps? Then it is rough.
flow.kid: Press with your thumb. Does it squash? Stroke with your finger. Can you feel bumps?

flow.do: Your child brings things from around the home, presses and strokes each one, and puts it by a slip.
flow.say: Find a hard thing. Now a soft thing. Now find something rough, and something smooth. How do you know?
flow.kid: Find a hard thing, a soft thing, a rough thing and a smooth thing. How do you know?

ask.q: How do you know the cushion is soft?
good: When I press it, it squashes.
My thumb goes in.

flow.parent: Good finds: a steel tumbler, a cushion, a coconut shell or doormat, a glass bottle. Some things fit two slips: a coconut shell is hard and rough. Put it between the slips.

flow.do: Pick up a pillow or cushion and ask the check question.
flow.say: Here is a pillow. Press it with your thumb. What is it like?
flow.kid: Press the pillow. What is it like?

check.q: You press a pillow and it squashes. What is the pillow like?
check.why: A soft thing changes shape when you press it. A hard thing does not.

activities.title: Crayon Rubbings: catch the bumps on paper
activities.context: In this activity you put thin paper on top of a surface and rub over it with the side of a crayon. Rough surfaces leave a pattern on the paper. Smooth ones leave a plain patch.

materials.item: thin paper, such as old notebook pages or printer paper
a crayon with the paper wrapper taken off
things to rub: a coin, a leaf, a comb, a doormat, a floor tile, a steel plate

schedule.what: Make rubbings of rough and smooth surfaces, then guess which rubbing came from which thing.

activities.record: Keep the rubbings. Write or draw under each one what it came from.

setup.art: A sheet of thin paper laid over a leaf on a table, and a child rubbing over it with the side of a green crayon, the leaf's veins showing through.
setup.caption: 1. Put paper on top. Rub with the side of a crayon.

setup.art: A sheet of rubbings: a coin pattern, leaf veins, the grid of a doormat, and a plain smooth patch from a steel plate.
setup.caption: 2. Rough things leave a pattern. Smooth things leave a plain patch.

flow.do: 1. Take the wrapper off the crayon. 2. Show your child how to hold the crayon on its side.
flow.say: We are going to make the bumps on things show up on paper. Hold the crayon on its side, like this.
flow.kid: Hold the crayon on its side. You will make the bumps on things show up on paper.

flow.do: Your child lays paper on each thing and rubs over it gently. Do at least one rough thing and one smooth thing.
flow.say: Before you rub the steel plate, guess. Will you see a pattern? Why? Now rub and see.
flow.kid: Put the paper on top. Guess: will a pattern show? Why? Now rub.

ask.q: Why did the doormat make a pattern, and the steel plate did not?
good: The doormat is bumpy. The bumps push up into the crayon.
The plate is smooth, so the colour is all the same.

flow.parent: Hold the paper still with one hand. Leaves work best with the veiny side up.

flow.do: Mix the rubbings up. Your child guesses which thing made each one.
flow.say: Here are your rubbings, all mixed up. Which one came from the leaf? How can you tell?
flow.kid: Look at a rubbing. Which thing made it? How can you tell?

check.q: Which surface would leave the plainest rubbing?
check.why: A smooth surface has no bumps big enough to push up into the crayon, so the colour comes out plain.

activities.title: The Gentle Bend: bendy or stiff?
activities.context: In this activity you try to bend things gently with your hands. Bendy things bend easily. Stiff things keep their shape.

materials.item: things to bend: a dupatta or hanky, a sheet of paper, a plastic ruler, a steel spoon, a pencil, a rubber chappal, a curry leaf or any leaf

schedule.what: Bend each thing gently and sort the bendy from the stiff.

activities.record: Draw a bendy thing bending, and a stiff thing staying straight.

setup.art: A row of things on a mat: a hanky, a sheet of paper, a plastic ruler, a steel spoon, a pencil and a rubber chappal.
setup.caption: 1. Put the things in a row.

setup.art: A girl gently bending a rubber chappal into a curve, with a steel spoon lying straight beside her.
setup.caption: 2. Bend each one gently. Bendy or stiff?

flow.do: Show your child how to bend gently with two hands. Agree that we never push hard enough to break anything.
flow.say: We bend gently, like this. If it bends easily, it is bendy. If it stays straight, it is stiff. We never push so hard that it breaks.
flow.kid: Bend each thing gently. Bendy or stiff? Never push hard.

flow.do: Your child guesses for each thing, then bends it gently, and puts it in a bendy pile or a stiff pile.
flow.say: Will the chappal bend? Why do you think so? Try it. Now the spoon.
flow.kid: Guess first. Bendy or stiff? Why? Now try.

ask.q: Is the ruler bendy or stiff?
good: A bit bendy. It bends a little and springs back.
It is in the middle.

flow.parent: The pencil and spoon are stiff. The hanky, paper, chappal and leaf are bendy. A plastic ruler bends a little, so it can go between the piles.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last question about bending.
flow.kid: Answer one question.

check.q: A steel spoon is stiff. A thin steel wire bends easily. Why?
options: The wire is made of cloth
check.why: Both are steel. A thin piece of a material bends more easily than a thick piece.

games.title: Run and Touch: find it fast
games.players: 1 or more players and one caller.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller reads a property card, and you run to touch something in the room that has that property.

items.b: It does not squash when you press it. A tumbler, a wall, a table.
It squashes when you press it. A pillow, a towel, your cheek.
You can feel bumps. A doormat, a coconut shell, a brick wall.
It feels flat and even. A mirror, a tile, a steel plate.
It bends easily. A dupatta, a chappal, a sheet of paper.
It keeps its shape. A pencil, a spoon, a door.
It reflects light back in one direction. A steel tumbler, a mirror, a phone screen.
It does not shine. A towel, a newspaper, a clay pot.

rules: The caller mixes the 8 property cards and reads one out loud.
Every player runs to touch something in the room that has that property.
Each player says what they touched, and how they know.
A good reason gets a point. A grown-up reads the cards for a caller who cannot read yet. If a player cannot find anything, the caller gives a hint.
Play until all 8 cards have been read. Then swap callers and play again. At the end, add up the points. The highest wins, or try to beat your own total next time.

setup.art: A woman holding up a card that says SHINY, and a girl running to touch a steel water bottle.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a card.

setup.art: A boy pressing his thumb into a sofa cushion, saying soft, while a girl touches a brick wall, saying rough.
setup.caption: 2. Run to touch it, then say how you know.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space. 2. Mix the cards. 3. Read the rules to your child.
flow.say: I will read a word. You run and touch something that is like that word. Then tell me how you know.
flow.kid: Listen to the word. Run and touch something like it. Say how you know.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. Your child runs, touches and explains.
flow.say: Shiny! Run and touch something shiny. How do you know it is shiny?
flow.kid: Run and touch it. How do you know?

ask.q: How do you know the tumbler is shiny?
good: I can see light on it.
I can see my face in it.

flow.parent: Ask for the test each time: pressing for soft, stroking for rough, bending gently for bendy, looking for shiny.

flow.do: Ask the check question. Then your child is the caller.
flow.say: Now you be the caller, and I will run.
flow.kid: Now you read the cards. A grown-up runs.

check.q: Which test tells you if a thing is rough?
check.why: Your finger feels the bumps on a rough surface. A smooth surface feels flat and even.

games.title: Guess My Thing: clues from properties
games.context: This is a guessing game. One player picks a secret thing from the home and gives clues using only property words. The others guess the thing.

items.b: Clues: hard, smooth, shiny, stiff.
Clues: soft, smooth, dull, bendy.
Clues: hard, rough, dull, stiff.
Clues: bendy, smooth, shiny.

img.credit: Lucas Christofides, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Clues: rough, hard, dull, a little stiff.
Clues: hard, very smooth, very shiny, stiff.
Clues: bendy, a little soft, dull.
Clues: hard, a little rough, dull, stiff.
Clues: soft, a little rough, bendy, dull.
Clues: very bendy, smooth, shiny.
Clues: hard, stiff, dull, a little rough.
Clues: soft, smooth, shiny when still.

rules: Mix the cards and put them face down.
The first player takes a card and keeps it secret. A grown-up whispers it to a player who cannot read yet.
The player gives one clue at a time, using only property words: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stiff, shiny or dull.
The others guess after each clue. Whoever guesses right gets a point and takes the next card. If nobody guesses after all the clues, show the card and let the next player take a card.
After the property clues, a player may add one more clue with a real thing: 'It is as rough as the doormat.'
Play until every player has had two turns, or the cards run out. The most points wins, or just count the family's total.

setup.art: A girl holding a card close to her chest, saying hard and shiny, while two friends think.
setup.caption: 1. Pick a secret card. Give one property clue.

setup.art: A boy calling out steel tumbler, and the girl turning her card over to show it.
setup.caption: 2. Guess after each clue.

flow.do: Read the rules. Play the first round yourself, so your child hears how clues sound.
flow.say: I have a secret thing. Here is my first clue. It is hard. Second clue. It is rough. Third clue. It is dull. What is it?
flow.kid: Listen to the clues. Guess the thing.
flow.parent: The first round is the coconut shell. Give the clues slowly.

flow.do: Take turns. Your child picks a card and gives clues. Help with words if they get stuck.
flow.say: Your turn. Look at your secret card. Give me one clue. Is it hard or soft?
flow.kid: Look at your card. Give one clue. Is it hard or soft?

good: Shiny, because only a few things are shiny.
Rough, because it stopped me guessing the tumbler.

flow.parent: Some cards surprise children. Water is soft and smooth, and shiny when still. Foil is shiny but very bendy.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: One last puzzle about clues.
flow.kid: Answer one question.

check.q: The clues are: hard, smooth, shiny. Which thing could it be?
check.why: A steel plate is hard, smooth and shiny. A towel is soft and dull, and a doormat is rough.

projects.title: My Feel Book: one property a day
projects.context: In this project you make a small book. Each day you find two things that are opposites, like hard and soft, and stick a small piece or a drawing of each on the pages.

materials.item: 4 sheets of paper, folded in half and tied with thread into a little book
glue or tape
small bits to stick: a scrap of cloth, foil, sandpaper or a bit of doormat, a thread, a leaf, a toothpick, a square of newspaper
crayons

schedule.what: Make the book. Fill the HARD and SOFT pages.
Fill the ROUGH and SMOOTH pages.
Fill the BENDY and STIFF pages.
Fill the SHINY and DULL pages. Show the book to someone, letting them touch each page.

projects.record: The finished book, with something to touch or see on every page.

setup.art: Four sheets of paper folded and tied with thread into a little book, with 'My Feel Book' on the cover.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and tie four sheets into a book.

setup.art: An open little book with a scrap of rough doormat stuck on one page and a square of shiny foil on the facing page.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, stick on two opposites.

flow.do: 1. Make the book. 2. Write HARD and SOFT on the first two pages. 3. Your child finds something for each, and sticks a small piece or draws it.
flow.say: This book will be full of things to feel. Today, find something hard and something soft. Can you stick a little piece on, or draw it?
flow.kid: Find something hard and something soft. Stick a bit on, or draw it.
flow.parent: A hard thing is often too big to stick, so a drawing is fine. A cotton ball or cloth scrap works well for soft.

flow.do: Write ROUGH and SMOOTH on the next pages. Your child sticks on a rough bit and a smooth bit.
flow.say: Today, rough and smooth. Find a rough bit to stick on, and a smooth bit. Stroke them with your finger.
flow.kid: Find a rough bit and a smooth bit. Stick them on. Stroke them.

flow.do: Write BENDY and STIFF on the next pages. Your child sticks on a thread or leaf for bendy, and a toothpick for stiff.
flow.say: Today, bendy and stiff. What can you stick on that bends? What stays straight?
flow.kid: Stick on something bendy and something stiff.

flow.do: Write SHINY and DULL on the last pages. Your child sticks on foil for shiny and newspaper for dull. Then they show the book to someone and tell them about each page.
flow.say: Last pages: shiny and dull. Then show your whole book to someone at home, or on a call. Tell them about each page, and let them touch every page they can.
flow.kid: Stick on something shiny and something dull. Show your book to someone and tell them about it.

challenges.title: A Mirror for a Doll
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a mirror for a doll or a toy, using things from home. A good mirror lets you see a face in it.
challenges.problem: A doll has no mirror. Can you make one from things at home? You must be able to see your face in it, even a little.
constraints: It must be small enough for a doll.
You must be able to see a face in it.
materials: a steel lid or a steel spoon
black paper and cling film or a clear plastic sheet
a small dark bowl of water
general: Real mirrors are glass with a thin layer of shiny metal behind or on top of it.
Aranmula mirrors from Kerala are metal, polished for days until they are very smooth.
Long before glass mirrors, people looked at their faces in still water.
creative: Press kitchen foil very flat onto a piece of card, so that it has no creases.
Use the back of a shiny steel spoon. Your face looks funny, because the spoon is curved.
Put clear plastic over black paper. It reflects only a little, so dim the room and look closely for a faint face.
challenges.your_turn: Make two different mirrors. Which one shows your face best? Why do you think so?

setup.art: A child smoothing a sheet of kitchen foil flat over a small piece of cardboard with the side of a hand.
setup.caption: 1. Make a small mirror from home things.

setup.art: A doll propped up facing a small foil-covered card, and a child comparing it with a steel lid.
setup.caption: 2. Which mirror shows a face best?

flow.do: Read the problem to your child.
flow.say: The doll has no mirror. Can we make one? What does a mirror need to be like, so we can see a face in it?
flow.kid: The doll needs a mirror. What must a mirror be like?

ask.q: What must a mirror be like?
good: Shiny.
Very smooth, like the steel plate in the Torch Spot Test.

flow.do: Your child makes two mirrors from the materials. Help smooth the foil.
flow.say: Smooth the foil very flat on the card. Rub it gently with your palm. Can you see your face? Now crumple a bit of it. What happens?
flow.kid: Make a mirror. Smooth the foil flat. Can you see your face?
flow.parent: Flat foil shows a blurry face. Crumpled foil shows none. The Torch Spot Test showed the same thing: smooth things shine, and bumpy things do not.

flow.do: Compare the mirrors. Your child picks the best one and gives a reason.
flow.say: Which mirror shows your face best? Why do you think that one works best?
flow.kid: Which mirror is best? Why?

items.p: Here are four things. Say one property word for each one, and a grown-up writes it: hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy, stiff, shiny or dull.
items.why: Many words can fit. A strong answer gives a word that the child could check by pressing, stroking, bending or looking.
items.art: A coconut shell, a small mirror, a pillow and a rubber chappal in a row, with an empty label under each.

items.p: Draw a line from each question to the test that answers it.
items.why: Each property has its own test. Pressing finds soft, stroking finds rough, bending finds bendy, and a torch finds shiny.
items.art: A pillow, a doormat, a chappal and a steel plate on the left, and a thumb, a finger, two bending hands and a torch on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Which of these would make a bright spot on the wall with a torch? Circle the shiny ones in yellow and the dull ones in brown.
items.why: Smooth steel, a mirror and still water reflect light back in one direction, so they make a spot. Newspaper, cloth and clay have tiny bumps that send the light off in all directions.

items.p: Draw the Torch Spot Test: the torch, the steel plate and the bright spot on the wall.
items.a: A torch shining at a slant onto a plate, and a bright spot on the wall.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the light going from the torch to the plate, and from the plate to the wall.
items.art: A blank box with a small table drawn at the bottom and a wall at the side.

items.p: A mirror makes its own light.
items.why: False. A mirror only sends back light that falls on it. In a dark room it does not shine.

items.p: Three of these are soft. Which one is not?
items.why: A pillow, a cotton ball and an idli squash when you press them. A steel spoon does not squash, so it is hard.

items.p: Many children think only metal things are shiny. Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it: which shiny things did you find that are not metal?
items.a: Still water, a glass bottle, a glazed cup, a banana leaf.
items.why: A strong answer names shiny things that are not metal and says what they share: a very smooth surface.

items.p: You smooth kitchen foil flat and see a blurry face in it. Then you crumple the foil into a ball. What will you see now?
items.why: Crumpled foil has many bumps and folds. They send the light off in many directions, so no face comes back.

items.p: Kavya and her friend Thenmozhi are looking at a bucket of water in Madurai.

views.says: Water is not shiny. You can see right through it. Only steel and mirrors are shiny.
Still water is shiny. In the Torch Spot Test it made a bright spot on the ceiling, and I can see my face in it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For Thenmozhi: the water made a bright spot, and it shows faces when still. For Kavya: you can see through water, and its spot was fainter than the mirror's.
items.why: Both girls see something true. Water lets most light through, so it shines less than a mirror. But its smooth surface still reflects some light back in one direction, so still water shines.

items.p: Draw one rough thing and one smooth thing from your home. Draw bumps on the rough one.
items.a: Two drawings, such as a doormat with bumps and a steel plate with none.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference you feel: bumps on the rough thing, an even surface on the smooth one.
items.art: A blank box split in two, labelled ROUGH and SMOOTH.

items.p: You fold your paper bridge so that the folds run across the gap, not from one pile of books to the other. How well will it hold coins?
opts: It sags with few coins, because folds must run from pile to pile
It holds the same as the zigzag bridge
It holds more than the zigzag bridge
items.why: Folds that run from pile to pile stop the paper bending downwards. Folds across the gap let it bend like a flat sheet.

items.p: A glass tumbler is hard, so it can never break.
items.why: False. Glass is hard because it does not squash when you press it. But it can shatter if it falls on the floor.

items.p: Think about bending each one gently. Is it bendy or stiff?
items.why: A dupatta, a chappal and paper bend easily. A pencil, a spoon and a door keep their shape.

items.p: Paper feels smooth to your finger. But in the Torch Spot Test it made no bright spot. Say why, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: Paper has tiny fibres and bumps, too small to feel. They send the light off in all directions.
items.why: A strong answer says that paper has bumps too small for a finger to feel, but big enough to spoil the shine.

items.p: A girl sees the sky in a river. Draw the river when it is still. Then draw it just after a boat goes past.
items.a: A still river with the sky in it, and a rippled river with the sky broken into pieces.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a clear sky in the smooth water, and broken pieces in the rippled water.
items.art: A blank box split in two, labelled STILL and AFTER THE BOAT.

items.p: Meera and her sister Anu are folding a cotton towel in Kochi.

views.says: This towel is soft. When I squeeze it, it squashes.
No, this towel is rough. When I rub it on my cheek, I feel little loops.

items.ask: Who is right? Why? Can they both be right?
items.a: Both are right. Soft and rough are two different properties. The towel squashes, so it is soft. Its surface has loops, so it is a little rough.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the girls did two different tests. Pressing tells you soft or hard. Stroking tells you rough or smooth. One thing can be soft and rough.

items.p: The sole of a chappal is rough underneath. Why is that useful?
opts: The bumps grip the floor, so your foot does not slip
The bumps make the chappal shine
The bumps make the chappal lighter
items.why: A rough surface has bumps that catch on the floor. A smooth sole slides more easily.

items.p: Here is a steel spoon. Next to each test, write what you would find out.
items.why: Each test finds one property. A steel spoon is hard, smooth, stiff and shiny.
items.art: A steel spoon in the middle, with four arrows going to a thumb, a finger, two bending hands and a torch, and an empty label by each.

items.p: Draw a line from each job to the property it needs most.
items.why: A pillow must squash under your head. A mirror must be smooth to show a face. A rough mat scrapes mud off. A chair leg must keep its shape under you.
items.art: A pillow, a mirror, a doormat and a chair on the left, and the words soft, smooth and shiny, rough, stiff on the right, mixed up.

items.p: A dull grey metal disc is rubbed for many days, until you can see your face in it. What changed?
opts: The surface of the metal became very smooth
items.why: It was the same metal all along. Rubbing took away the tiny bumps, so the smooth surface reflected light back in one direction.

quiz.p: You press your thumb on a steel tumbler. Nothing squashes. What is the tumbler like?
quiz.why: A hard thing does not change shape when you press it.

quiz.p: You stroke a doormat and feel lots of bumps. What is the doormat like?
quiz.why: Bumps you can feel make a surface rough.

quiz.p: What do we call words like hard, soft, rough and shiny?
quiz.why: Properties tell us what a material is like. A material is what a thing is made of.

quiz.p: A steel tumbler is a thing. What is steel?
opts: The material it is made of
quiz.why: Steel is the material. Shiny and hard are its properties.
A very smooth surface reflects light back in one direction. A mirror does not make light. In a dark room it does not shine.

quiz.p: You splash a bucket of still water. Your face in the water breaks into pieces. Why?
opts: The ripples make the surface bumpy
quiz.why: Ripples make the water's surface bumpy, so the light goes off in many directions. When the water is still again, your face comes back.

quiz.p: Which of these is shiny but is NOT made of metal?
quiz.why: Glass is very smooth, so it shines. Steel and brass are metals.

quiz.p: Cardboard boxes have a wavy layer of paper inside. Why?
opts: The waves make the card stiff
The waves make the card shiny
The waves make the card softer
quiz.why: A wavy layer is like the zigzag paper bridge. The shape makes thin paper stiff.

quiz.p: You guess that the hanky will make a bright spot in the Torch Spot Test. It does not. What should you do?
opts: Say what you saw, and change your idea
Keep your guess, because it was yours
quiz.why: A guess is where a test starts. When the test shows something else, a scientist says what she saw and changes her idea.

quiz.p: Why do we hold the torch at the same slant for each thing in the Torch Spot Test?
opts: So the test is fair for each thing
So the torch does not get hot
quiz.why: If only one thing changes each time, we know that thing made the difference.

applications: Cooks choose soft, bendy banana leaves to serve and wrap food, and hard steel for pots.
Shoemakers make chappal soles rough underneath, so they grip the floor.
Mirror makers polish metal or coat glass to make a very smooth, shiny surface.
Lines painted on roads have tiny glass beads in the paint, so they shine back at car headlights at night.

spotted.text: A banana leaf at a meal in Kerala or Tamil Nadu, shiny and smooth on top.
spotted.art: A banana leaf on a table with rice, sambar and payasam, the leaf's surface catching the light.

spotted.text: Steel tiffin boxes on a dabbawala's crate in Mumbai, shining in the sun.
spotted.art: A dabbawala in a white cap carrying a long crate of shining steel tiffin boxes.

spotted.text: The rough coir doormat at the door of a flat in Kochi, made from coconut husk.
spotted.art: A brown coir doormat at a flat's front door, with a pair of chappals beside it.

spotted.text: A still lake in Udaipur after sunset, shining with the lights of the city.
spotted.art: A calm lake at dusk with palace lights reflected in the still water.

spotted.text: A bamboo basket at a market in Assam: stiff when woven, though each thin strip is bendy.
spotted.art: A woman in a mekhela chador holding up a woven bamboo basket at a market stall.

open_questions.q: Why do people like shiny things so much?
open_questions.why_open: Many people choose shiny things over dull ones. One idea is that shine reminds us of water, which every animal needs. Scientists are still testing this, and nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: How does your skin know a thing is soft?
open_questions.why_open: Tiny sensors in the skin feel pressing and stretching. But how the body puts all their messages together into 'soft' is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can we make a material that is very hard and very bendy at once?
open_questions.why_open: Hard things are often stiff, and bendy things are often soft. Scientists keep trying to make new materials that are both, and the search is not finished.

ask_kids: What is the softest thing in this room? How do you know?
Can you find something shiny in the kitchen? Is it smooth?
Is your chappal bendy or stiff? Try it.
Where in your home can you find something both soft and rough?
Is your hair rough or smooth? Is your cheek?
What would happen if a pillow was hard?

jokes.j: Why did the mirror get top marks?
jokes.a: Because it always reflects before it answers!

jokes.j: What did the pillow say to the stone?
jokes.a: Don't be so hard on yourself!

jokes.j: Why was the sandpaper never invited to parties?
jokes.a: It was too rough with everyone!

jokes.j: What did the steel plate say after you breathed on it?
jokes.a: I'm feeling a bit dull today!

jokes.j: Why did the chappal win the yoga contest?
jokes.a: It was the bendiest one there!

jokes.j: What did one floor tile say to the other?
Why did the pencil feel left out?
jokes.a: Everyone else bent the rules, but it was too stiff!

jokes.j: What is the shiniest day of the week?

maths.problem: In the Torch Spot Test, you tested 7 things. 4 of them made a bright spot. How many made no spot?
maths.explain: Take the 4 that made a spot away from the 7 things. That leaves 3. So 3 things made no spot.
maths.context: This is about the Torch Spot Test, where you shone a torch on things from home.
maths.why_maths: Taking away tells us how many things were dull, without counting them all again.

maths.problem: The flat paper bridge held 1 coin. The zigzag bridge held 9 coins. Which bridge held more? How many more?
maths.answer: The zigzag bridge held 8 more coins.
maths.explain: 9 is more than 1. Count on from 1 to 9: that is 8 more. So the folds made the paper hold many more coins.
maths.context: This is about the Paper Bridge test, where you folded paper into a zigzag.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows how big a difference the fold made.

maths.problem: Put these in two hoops on the floor: HARD and SHINY. A steel spoon, a mirror, a wooden spoon, a coconut shell, a sheet of foil. Which things go in both hoops at once?
maths.answer: The steel spoon and the mirror.
maths.explain: The steel spoon and the mirror are hard and shiny, so they go where the hoops cross. The wooden spoon and coconut shell are hard but dull. The foil is shiny but bendy, not hard.
maths.context: This is about sorting things by two properties at once.
maths.why_maths: Two overlapping hoops show at a glance which things share both properties.

warmup.q: Is a pillow hard or soft?
warmup.a: Soft. It squashes when you press it.

warmup.q: Is a coconut shell rough or smooth?
warmup.a: Rough. You can feel bumps and hairs.

warmup.q: Is a pencil bendy or stiff?
Name something in your kitchen that is shiny.
warmup.a: A steel plate, a tumbler or foil. Shiny things have a very smooth surface.
Yes, when it is still and smooth.

warmup.q: Is a banana leaf bendy or stiff?

roots.context: We have pressed, stroked, bent and shone a torch on things from home. Now we look at what we learn from the steel plate that went dull under a breath and then shone again.

deep_truth.truth: You breathed on a cold, shiny steel plate, and it went dull. A few seconds later it shone again. The steel never changed: tiny drops of water had made its surface bumpy. So a very smooth surface shines, whether it is steel, glass or still water.
deep_truth.habit: We think of shiny as something only some materials are, like metal. The test shows that shine belongs to the surface. The same steel was dull and then shiny, and plain water shone too.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Torch Spot Test, the cold plate's bright spot faded under a breath and came back as the mist dried. Still water made a spot, and ripples broke it up. Newspaper, which feels smooth, made no spot.

three.who_am_i: You find out what the world is like through your fingers and eyes. Your own skin is soft, bendy and a little rough.
three.what_is_life: Living beings have surfaces too. A banana leaf is smooth and shiny, a coconut's husk is rough, and a cat's fur is soft.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of surfaces, and light bounces off every one. How smooth a surface is decides whether it shines.

roots.thread: Steel, glass, water and a banana leaf are very different things. Yet they all shine for the same reason: their surfaces are very smooth. Everything is conscious, and each of them meets the light in its own way.

teachings.teaching: As fire is covered by smoke, and a mirror is covered by dust, so knowing is covered by wanting.
teachings.link: In the Gita the shine of a mirror is not lost under dust, only covered. In our test, mist covered the steel plate, and the shine came back when the mist dried.

teachings.source: The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, chapter 1
teachings.teaching: The monk Shenxiu wrote that the mind is like a bright mirror, and we must wipe it often so that dust does not settle. The young helper Huineng answered that the bright mirror has no stand, so where could dust land?
teachings.link: Both verses use a mirror, because a mirror shines only while its surface is clear and smooth. The two monks argued about what keeps the mind clear, and Buddhists still talk about it.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing away what is hard.
teachings.link: Water is soft: your finger goes right into it. Yet drops falling for many years wear hollows into hard stone steps. Soft and hard can meet, and the soft one can win.

science.text: A smooth surface reflects light back in one direction, so we see a shine or a clear picture. A rough surface sends light off in many directions, so it looks dull.
Why people are drawn to shiny things is still being studied. One idea is that shine reminds us of water.

other_view.view: Many scientists say that shine is only light bouncing off a surface, and nothing more is going on in the steel. For them, feeling belongs to living beings with nerves.

practice.title: Watch the mist go
practice.say: Take a steel spoon or plate that has been in the fridge for 10 minutes. Hold it close to your face. Breathe out slowly onto it, 'haaa'. Now stay very still and watch. See the mist shrink from the edges. Breathe in slowly while it goes. When it has gone, look at the shine. The steel was the same steel all the time.
practice.kid: Breathe 'haaa' on a spoon from the fridge. Stay still. Watch the mist shrink away. Breathe in slowly. See the shine come back.

ask: When the plate was misty, was it still the same steel?
Name something dull that could shine if it were smoother.
Why do you think so many people love shiny things?
roots.art: A girl holding a steel spoon close to her face, a small mist on the spoon shrinking from the edges, and her calm face reflected in the clear middle.

how_we_found_out.story: For about 200 years, the best telescopes used mirrors made of thick discs of metal. Isaac Newton made one of the first, in 1668. In England, in the 1770s and 1780s, Caroline Herschel helped her brother William make many more. Polishing one mirror could take many hours without a break, so Caroline fed William by hand while he polished. She also found comets, and became one of the first women ever paid to do science. But metal mirrors had a problem. In damp air they slowly went dull, and had to be polished all over again. In 1835, the German chemist Justus von Liebig found a way to lay a very thin layer of silver onto glass. In 1856 and 1857, Carl August von Steinheil in Germany and Léon Foucault in France made telescope mirrors this way. A smooth glass disc with a thin silver skin shone better than solid metal. Today, big telescope mirrors are glass with a layer of aluminium far thinner than a hair. The shine is all in the surface.
how_we_found_out.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist; Caroline Herschel, a German-born astronomer in England, and her brother William; Justus von Liebig, a German chemist; Carl August von Steinheil, a German scientist; Léon Foucault, a French scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a good telescope mirror had to be a thick disc of solid metal. In fact, thin silver on smooth glass shone better.

founder: ideas/by_topic/materials-and-their-properties.md: the founder's painting idea for textures (rough wood grain, shiny metal, soft fabric) grew into the crayon rubbings and the Feel Book. The sound, transparency and heat activities belong to other units. The Level 3 unit uses the feely bag, the snap and droop tests, the damp strength test, the vanishing drop and the transparency layers, and Level 2 testing uses the stretch and waterproof tests, so this unit uses the touch hunt, the torch spot test, the breath on a cold plate, the paper bridge and crayon rubbings instead.
Combined lesson sci-C1-materials-and-their-properties: the property words hard, soft, rough, smooth, bendy and stiff, and its warm-up idea of naming the material of everyday things.
science: Reflection: a smooth surface gives specular (mirror-like) reflection, and a rough surface gives diffuse reflection. Any introductory optics text.
Isaac Newton's reflecting telescope, 1668, with a speculum metal mirror (an alloy of copper and tin).
Caroline Herschel's memoir describes feeding her brother William by hand while he polished a mirror for many hours. In 1787 King George III gave her a salary as his assistant.
Justus von Liebig's silvering of glass (1835), and the silvered-glass telescope mirrors of Carl August von Steinheil (1856) and Léon Foucault (1857).
Aranmula kannadi: hand-made metal mirrors from Aranmula, Kerala, cast from a copper and tin alloy and polished by hand. They have a Geographical Indication tag.
Katrien Meert, Mario Pandelaere and Vanessa Patrick, 'Taking a shine to it', Journal of Consumer Psychology 24 (2014): the idea that the liking for glossy things is linked to a need for water.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project and challenge as a parent and child in a flat, at 2 and at 4 players, checking printables, minutes and schedules. Fixed: the cold plate would mist by itself in humid weather and was shown too early, so the steps now keep it in the fridge, wipe it dry and say what a scratched plate gives; the doormat clue now agrees with the Touch Hunt; the story is shorter, with the repeated water scene and the extra child cut; the roots practice no longer says the shine hides under mist; and repeated questions (foil mirror, cold plate, paper fold, cardboard) were replaced with new ones. Video ids are still to find.
